claim: The central axis of motor and nonmotor macroscale organization in the cerebellum remains unknown.
source: In contrast, and despite its growing importance in basic and clinical neuroscience, the central axis of motor and nonmotor macroscale organization in the cerebellum remains unknown.
evidence: This is stated as a knowledge gap in the introduction, contrasting with the known organization of the cerebral cortex.

claim: The human cerebellum is engaged not only in motor control but also in cognitive and affective processing.
source: In addition to anatomy, evidence from clinical, behavioral and neuroimaging studies indicates that the human cerebellum is engaged not only in motor control but also in cognitive and affective processing (Schmahmann and Pandya, 1991; Schmahmann, 1996; Baillieux et al., 2008; Stoodley and Schmahmann, 2009; Thompson and Steinmetz, 2009; Tedesco et al., 2011; Stoodley et al., 2012; E et al., 2014; Koziol et al., 2014; Guell et al., 2015; Hoche et al., 2016, 2018; Schmahmann and Pandya, 1997a, Schmahmann and Pandya, 1997b1997b; Middleton and Strick, 1994; Schmahmann and Sherman, 1998; Levisohn et al., 2000; Riva and Giorgi, 2000; Ravizza et al., 2006; Schmahmann et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by extensive citations to clinical, behavioral, and neuroimaging studies.

claim: There are no cerebellar cortical association fibers.
source: The fact that there are no cerebellar cortical association fibers (Schmahmann, 1996; Schmahmann and Pandya, 2008) makes it difficult to analyze intra-cerebellar progressive hierarchical relationships using anatomical techniques.
evidence: Supported by citations to anatomical studies by Schmahmann and colleagues.

claim: Gradient 1 explained the largest part of variability in resting-state connectivity patterns within the cerebellum.
source: Gradient 1 explained the largest part of variability in resting-state connectivity patterns within the cerebellum (Figure 1A).
evidence: Directly stated in the results and shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Gradient 1 extended bilaterally from lobules IV/V/VI and lobule VIII to posterior aspects of Crus I and Crus II as well as medial regions of lobule IX.
source: It extended bilaterally from lobules IV/V/VI and lobule VIII to posterior aspects of Crus I and Crus II as well as medial regions of lobule IX.
evidence: Directly stated in the results describing Gradient 1.

claim: Gradient 1 is anchored at one end by cerebellar motor regions and at the other end by regions engaged in the language task.
source: Overlap with task activity maps (Figure 1B) revealed that Gradient 1 is anchored at one end by cerebellar motor regions and at the other end by regions engaged in the language task of the HCP dataset.
evidence: Directly stated in results and shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Gradient 1 extends from sensorimotor network to DMN regions of the cerebellum.
source: Overlap with cerebellar representations of cerebral cortical resting-state networks (Figure 1B) revealed that Gradient 1 extends from sensorimotor network to DMN regions of the cerebellum.
evidence: Directly stated in results and shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Ventral/dorsal attention and frontoparietal networks were situated between the two extreme ends of Gradient 1.
source: Ventral/dorsal attention and frontoparietal networks were situated between the two extreme ends.
evidence: Directly stated in results describing Gradient 1.

claim: Gradient 2 included at one end the anterior portions of Crus I and Crus II bilaterally.
source: Gradient 2, the component accounting for the second-most variance, included at one end the anterior portions of Crus I and Crus II bilaterally (Figure 1A).
evidence: Directly stated in results and shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The anterior portions of Crus I and Crus II corresponded to areas engaged in the HCP working-memory task.
source: These regions corresponded to areas engaged in the HCP working-memory task (Figure 1B).
evidence: Directly stated in results and shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The other end of Gradient 2 included both regions involved in motor processing and regions involved in language processing.
source: The other end of Gradient 2 included both regions involved in motor processing and regions involved in language processing; these areas correspond, respectively, to sensorimotor network and DMN regions.
evidence: Directly stated in results describing Gradient 2.

claim: Functional gradients calculated using functional connectivity values from the cerebellum to the cerebral cortex revealed a remarkably similar distribution to intra-cerebellar gradients.
source: Functional gradients calculated using functional connectivity values from the cerebellum to the cerebral cortex (rather than from the cerebellum to the cerebellum) revealed a remarkably similar distribution (Figure 2).
evidence: Directly stated in results and shown in Figure 2.

claim: Second motor representation (lobule VIII) and third nonmotor representations (lobule IX/X) were consistently located at less extreme positions along Gradient 1 and/or 2 when compared to their first motor and first/second nonmotor representations.
source: Second motor representation (lobule VIII) and third nonmotor representations (lobule IX/X) were consistently located at less extreme positions along Gradient 1 and/or 2 when compared to their first motor and first/second nonmotor representations, respectively.
evidence: Directly stated in results describing the analysis of motor and nonmotor representations.

claim: Cerebellar functional regions follow a gradual organization which progresses from primary (motor) to transmodal (DMN, task-unfocused) regions.
source: Here we applied diffusion map embedding to resting-state data from the Human Connectome Project dataset (n = 1003), and show for the first time that cerebellar functional regions follow a gradual organization which progresses from primary (motor) to transmodal (DMN, task-unfocused) regions.
evidence: Directly stated in the abstract as a main finding.

claim: A secondary axis extends from task-unfocused to task-focused processing.
source: A secondary axis extends from task-unfocused to task-focused processing.
evidence: Directly stated in the abstract as a main finding.

claim: Functional differences exist not only between the two motor but also between the three nonmotor representations.
source: Functional differences exist not only between the two motor but also between the three nonmotor representations, and second motor representation might share functional similarities with third nonmotor representation.
evidence: Directly stated in the abstract as a main finding.

claim: Second motor representation might share functional similarities with third nonmotor representation.
source: Functional differences exist not only between the two motor but also between the three nonmotor representations, and second motor representation might share functional similarities with third nonmotor representation.
evidence: Stated as a speculative finding in the abstract.

claim: The cerebellum has a double motor representation in lobules I-VI and VIII.
source: Resting-state as well as task processing analyses have revealed a cerebellar double motor (lobules I-VI and VIII) and triple non-motor representation (lobules VI/Crus I, Crus II/VIIB and IX/X) (Buckner et al., 2011; Guell et al., 2018a)
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The cerebellum has a triple nonmotor representation in lobules VI/Crus I, Crus II/VIIB, and IX/X.
source: Resting-state as well as task processing analyses have revealed a cerebellar double motor (lobules I-VI and VIII) and triple non-motor representation (lobules VI/Crus I, Crus II/VIIB and IX/X) (Buckner et al., 2011; Guell et al., 2018a)
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: This is the first study to investigate the progressive, hierarchical organization of the cerebellum.
source: This is the first study to investigate the progressive, hierarchical organization of the cerebellum.
evidence: Directly stated in the discussion.

claim: Cerebellar macroscale organization is sensorimotor-fugal.
source: This is the first study to report a sensorimotor-fugal macroscale organization in the cerebellum; that is, a hierarchical organization that progresses away from sensorimotor function.
evidence: Directly stated in the discussion as a main finding.

claim: Cerebellum and cerebral cortex share a similar macroscale principle of organization.
source: This finding strongly suggests that cerebellum and cerebral cortex share a similar macroscale principle of organization, namely, that both structures share a hierarchical organization which gradually progresses away from unimodal streams of information processing.
evidence: Stated as an inference from the data comparing cerebellar and cortical gradients.

claim: The overlap between language task activity and DMN may be due to the language task contrast which subtracted listening to stories minus answering arithmetic questions.
source: The overlap between language task activity and DMN may be due to the language task contrast which subtracted listening to stories minus answering arithmetic questions.
evidence: Stated as an interpretation of the observed overlap.

claim: Working memory represents a nonmotor task which is not as distant from motor function as a story listening task.
source: It is reasonable to conceptualize working memory as a nonmotor task which is not as distant from motor function as a story listening task, justifying its middle position along Gradient 1.
evidence: Stated as a conceptual interpretation of the data.

claim: DMN and ventral/dorsal attention networks are two opposing brain systems.
source: Ventral and dorsal attention networks were located far from DMN along Gradient 1 (Figure 1B), consistent with the view that DMN and ventral/dorsal attention networks are two opposing brain systems (Fox et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to Fox et al. and observed in the data.

claim: The frontoparietal network is conceptualized as a mediator between DMN and ventral/dorsal attention networks.
source: The frontoparietal network is conceptualized as a mediator between the two (Vincent et al., 2008), justifying its position between ventral/dorsal attention networks and DMN along Gradient 1 (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by citation to Vincent et al. and observed in the data.

claim: The cerebellum does not show functional connectivity with primary visual or auditory cortices.
source: Of note, the cerebellum does not show functional connectivity with primary visual or auditory cortices (Buckner et al., 2011), but is anatomically and functionally connected with areas of primary sensorimotor processing and consistently engaged in simple motor tasks.
evidence: Supported by citation to Buckner et al.

claim: The cerebellum is anatomically and functionally connected with areas of primary sensorimotor processing.
source: Of note, the cerebellum does not show functional connectivity with primary visual or auditory cortices (Buckner et al., 2011), but is anatomically and functionally connected with areas of primary sensorimotor processing and consistently engaged in simple motor tasks.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge.

claim: The cerebellum is consistently engaged in simple motor tasks.
source: Of note, the cerebellum does not show functional connectivity with primary visual or auditory cortices (Buckner et al., 2011), but is anatomically and functionally connected with areas of primary sensorimotor processing and consistently engaged in simple motor tasks.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge.

claim: There are no short or long cerebellar cortical association fibers linking adjacent or distant cerebellar cortical areas with each other.
source: Unlike the cerebral cortex, there are no short or long cerebellar cortical association fibers linking adjacent or distant cerebellar cortical areas with each other (Schmahmann, 1996; Schmahmann and Pandya, 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to anatomical studies.

claim: The functional organization of the cerebellum is a consequence of the arrangement of cerebello-cerebral anatomical connections.
source: Our hypothesis is that such a functional organization is a consequence of the arrangement of cerebello-cerebral anatomical connections which in turn affect correlations in resting-state activity between cerebellar regions.
evidence: Stated as a hypothesis to explain the observed functional organization.

claim: Gradient 1 and Gradient 2 classify information processing in the cerebellum along two dimensions: distance from motor processing (Gradient 1) and amount of task-focus (Gradient 2).
source: In this way, Gradient 1 and Gradient 2 classify information processing in the cerebellum along two dimensions: distance from motor processing (Gradient 1) and amount of task-focus (Gradient 2).
evidence: Stated as an interpretation of the two gradients.

claim: HCP motor task is situated at a minimal position in Gradient 1 (i.e. maximally motor) and at a minimal position in Gradient 2 (i.e. minimally task-focused).
source: HCP motor task is situated at a minimal position in Gradient 1 (i.e. maximally motor) and at a minimal position in Gradient 2 (i.e. minimally task-focused) (Figure 1B).
evidence: Directly stated and shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Working memory is situated at a maximum position in Gradient 2.
source: The isolated cognitive process is closely related to task focus and is therefore situated at a maximum position in Gradient 2.
evidence: Stated as an interpretation of the working memory task position.

claim: There are no cerebellar voxels with simultaneous maximum Gradient 1 and Gradient 2 values.
source: First, there are no cerebellar voxels with simultaneous maximum Gradient 1 and Gradient 2 values.
evidence: Stated as an observation from the data distribution.

claim: There are no cerebellar voxels with simultaneous minimum Gradient 1 and maximum Gradient 2 values.
source: Second, there are no cerebellar voxels with simultaneous minimum Gradient 1 and maximum Gradient 2 values.
evidence: Stated as an observation from the data distribution.

claim: The distribution of Gradient 1 confirms the double motor/triple nonmotor organization.
source: The distribution of Gradient 1, the component that explains the greatest variability in resting-state intra-cerebellar connectivity patterns, confirms this organization.
evidence: Stated as a confirmation of previous findings.

claim: Gradient 1 lowest values correspond to lobules IV/V/VI and VIII.
source: Gradient 1 lowest values correspond to lobules IV/V/VI and VIII (Figure 1A, dark blue regions in Gradient 1), demarcating the two areas of motor representation.
evidence: Directly stated and shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The highest values of Gradient 1 correspond to lobules Crus I, Crus II, and lobule IX.
source: The highest values correspond to lobules Crus I, Crus II, and lobule IX (Figure 1A, dark red regions in Gradient 1) - these regions correspond to the first, contiguous second, and third nonmotor representation areas, respectively.
evidence: Directly stated and shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The double motor/triple nonmotor organization has been shown in cerebellar representations of cerebral resting-state networks, cerebellar task activity, cerebro-cerebellar functional connectivity from cerebral cortical task activity peaks, and gradients of intra-cerebellar patterns of functional connectivity.
source: Taken together, the double motor/triple nonmotor organization has now been shown in cerebellar representations of cerebral resting-state networks (Buckner et al., 2011), cerebellar task activity (Guell et al., 2018a), cerebro-cerebellar functional connectivity from cerebral cortical task activity peaks (Guell et al., 2018a), and gradients of intra-cerebellar patterns of functional connectivity (the present study).
evidence: Stated as a summary of evidence from multiple studies including the present one.

claim: Each nonmotor cerebellar network consists of three representations spanning VI/Crus I, Crus II/VIIB and IX/X.
source: Just as 'each distributed network consists of association areas spanning frontal, parietal, temporal and cingulate cortices' (Mesulam, 1981), the data indicate that each nonmotor cerebellar network consists of three representations spanning VI/Crus I, Crus II/VIIB and IX/X.
evidence: Stated as an interpretation of the data by analogy to cerebral cortex organization.

claim: Lobules I-VI and VIII receive input from and project to M1.
source: This conclusion is based on shared cerebello-cerebral cortical loops: lobules I-VI and VIII receive input from and project to M1, and lobules Crus I/Crus II and IX/X receive input from and project to area 46 (Kelly and Strick, 2003).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kelly and Strick.

claim: Lobules Crus I/Crus II and IX/X receive input from and project to area 46.
source: This conclusion is based on shared cerebello-cerebral cortical loops: lobules I-VI and VIII receive input from and project to M1, and lobules Crus I/Crus II and IX/X receive input from and project to area 46 (Kelly and Strick, 2003).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kelly and Strick.

claim: The contribution of the second motor representation (lobule VIII) is different from the contribution of the first motor representation (lobules I-VI).
source: This observation indicates that the contribution of the second motor representation (lobule VIII) is different from the contribution of the first motor representation (lobules I-VI), as expected from previous clinical (Stoodley et al., 2016; Schmahmann et al., 2009) and functional connectivity (Kipping et al., 2013) observations.
evidence: Stated as a conclusion from the data, supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The contribution of the third nonmotor representation (lobules IX/X) is different from the contribution of the first and second nonmotor representations (lobules VI/Crus I/Crus II/VIIB).
source: Crucially, it also indicates that the contribution of the third nonmotor representation (lobules IX/X) is different from the contribution of the first and second nonmotor representations (lobules VI/Crus I/Crus II/VIIB).
evidence: Stated as a novel conclusion from the data.

claim: A less extreme position along Gradient 1 and/or 2 in both third nonmotor and second motor representation represents a less extreme level of information processing.
source: We further speculate that a less extreme position along Gradient 1 and/or 2 in both third nonmotor and second motor representation represents, in both cases, a less extreme level of information processing.
evidence: Stated as a speculation based on the observed data patterns.

claim: Nonmotor activity in lobules IX and X might emerge from, and follow the logic of, motor processing in lobule VIII.
source: Because this pattern of a less extreme level of information processing is observed in both second motor representation and third nonmotor representation, we argue that nonmotor activity in lobules IX and X (third nonmotor representation) might emerge from, and follow the logic of, motor processing in lobule VIII (second motor representation).
evidence: Stated as a speculative interpretation of the observed pattern.

claim: The second representation of motor task activity, sensorimotor network, and 'Low-G1' maps were consistently located at a higher position along Gradient 2 when compared to their first representation.
source: The data show that the second representation of motor task activity, sensorimotor network, and 'Low-G1' (motor) maps were consistently located at a higher position along Gradient 2 when compared to their first representation.
evidence: Directly stated as an observation from the data.

claim: While the first motor representation is engaged in pure motor processing, second motor representation is engaged in motor processes that require higher task focus.
source: This suggests that while the first motor representation is engaged in pure motor processing as isolated by the Movement (e.g. tap left fingers) minus Average (average of the other four movements) contrast, second motor representation is engaged in motor processes that require higher task focus.
evidence: Stated as an interpretation of the observed position differences.

claim: Third representation of language task, DMN, and 'High-G1' maps were consistently located at a lower position along Gradient 1 when compared to their first and contiguous second representations.
source: Following a similar logic, third representation of language task, DMN, and 'High-G1' maps were consistently located at a lower position along Gradient 1 when compared to their first and contiguous second representations.
evidence: Directly stated as an observation from the data.

claim: The third representation of working memory, frontoparietal network, and 'High-G2' maps were consistently located at a lower position along Gradient 2 when compared to their first and second representations.
source: Also consistent with this logic, the third representation of working memory, frontoparietal network, and 'High-G2' maps were consistently located at a lower position along Gradient 2 when compared to their first and second representations.
evidence: Directly stated as an observation from the data.

claim: PICA occlusion commonly results in the infarction of lobule VIII but not of lobules IV/V/VI.
source: PICA occlusion commonly results in the infarction of lobule VIII (second motor representation) but not of lobules IV/V/VI (first motor representation).
evidence: Stated as clinical knowledge.

claim: PICA lesions result in little or no motor deficits.
source: Notably, these lesions result in little or no motor deficits (Stoodley et al., 2016; Schmahmann et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to clinical studies.

claim: The principal target of pontine visual cells in monkeys is lobule IX.
source: Glickstein and colleagues (Glickstein et al., 1994) reported that the principal target of pontine visual cells in monkeys is lobule IX.
evidence: Supported by citation to Glickstein et al.

claim: Calretinin-positive unipolar brush cells are preferentially located in lobules IX and X in many species.
source: A specific type of cell, the Calretinin-positive unipolar brush cell, is preferentially located in lobules IX and X in many species (Diño et al., 1999; Mugnaini et al., 2011) and receives vestibular afferents (Diño et al., 2001).
evidence: Supported by citations to anatomical studies.

claim: Lobules IX and X are classically considered to represent the vestibulocerebellum.
source: Accordingly, lobules IX and X are classically considered to represent the vestibulocerebellum.
evidence: Stated as established knowledge.

claim: The study analyzed data from 1003 participants of the Human Connectome Project.
source: Our analyses included data from 1003 participants of the Human Connectome Project (HCP) (Van Essen et al., 2013).
evidence: Directly stated in the results section.

claim: Each HCP participant provided one full hour of resting-state data.
source: We took advantage of the newly available and unparalleled power of the Human Connectome Project (HCP) dataset, where each participant (n = 1003) provided one full hour of resting-state data.
evidence: Directly stated in the introduction.

claim: Task activity maps included motor, working memory, emotion, social, and language processing from 787 participants.
source: We incorporated task activity maps (motor, working memory, emotion, social, and language processing) from a previously analyzed subset of the same group of participants (Guell et al., 2018a) (n = 787).
evidence: Directly stated in the introduction.

claim: Maps of cerebellar representation of cerebral cortical resting-state networks were obtained from Buckner et al. (2011) calculated in 1000 participants.
source: Maps of cerebellar representation of cerebral cortical resting-state networks were obtained from the study of Buckner et al. (2011), calculated in a different group of participants (n = 1000).
evidence: Directly stated in the introduction.

claim: Diffusion map embedding is a nonlinear dimensionality reduction technique.
source: Diffusion map embedding is a nonlinear dimensionality reduction technique and can be used to analyze similarities between functional connectivity based networks.
evidence: Stated as a description of the method.

claim: The initial dense connectome matrix includes the profile of connectivity of each cerebellar voxel with the rest of the cerebellum only.
source: It is important to highlight that our initial dense connectome matrix includes the profile of connectivity of each cerebellar voxel with the rest of the cerebellum only, rather than with the rest of the brain.
evidence: Directly stated in the methods section.

claim: The analysis reflects the intrinsic organization of the cerebellum without invoking its connectivity profiles with the cerebral hemispheres or other brain structures.
source: In this way, our analysis reflects the intrinsic organization of the cerebellum without invoking its connectivity profiles with the cerebral hemispheres or other brain structures.
evidence: Stated as a methodological feature of the analysis.

claim: Clustering of connectivity gradients revealed discrete networks similar to cerebello-cerebral connectivity parcellations from Buckner et al. (2011).
source: In addition, clustering of connectivity gradients revealed discrete networks similar to cerebello-cerebral connectivity parcellations from Buckner et al. (2011) (Figure 1—figure supplement 5).
evidence: Directly stated and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5.

claim: A similar distribution of gradients 1 and 2 could be observed when analyzing concatenated dataseries from a group of 32 participants.
source: Top row: Gradients 1 and 2 could also be observed when analyzing concatenated dataseries from a group of 32 participants, highlighting the applicability of our methodology to group studies with small cohorts of unrelated subjects.
evidence: Stated in the legend of Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: Gradients with a distribution similar to gradient 1 could be observed in most cases (29 out of 32 participants) when calculating gradients within each individual participant.
source: Bottom row: When calculating gradients within each individual participant of this subgroup and evaluating any of the first four resulting gradients, gradients with a distribution similar to gradient 1 could be observed in most cases (29 out of 32 participants).
evidence: Stated in the legend of Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: Gradients with a distribution similar to gradient 2 could be observed in half of the participants.
source: Gradients with a distribution similar to gradient 2 could be observed in half of the participants.
evidence: Stated in the legend of Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: Gradients 3 and 4 revealed laterality asymmetries in areas of nonmotor processing but not in areas of motor processing.
source: Gradients 3 and 4 revealed laterality asymmetries in areas of nonmotor processing (Crus I, Crus II, VIIB and IX) but not in areas of motor processing (IV/V/VI and VIII).
evidence: Stated in the legend of Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Left/right asymmetries in cerebellar processing have been described in multiple nonmotor tasks but not in motor processing.
source: Consistent with this observation, left/right asymmetries in cerebellar processing have been described in multiple nonmotor tasks (Hu et al., 2008) but not in motor processing.
evidence: Supported by citation to Hu et al.

claim: Connectivity from first motor representation corresponds to cerebral cortical somatomotor network.
source: These analyses are shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 5: while connectivity from first motor representation corresponds to cerebral cortical somatomotor network, connectivity from second motor representation engages areas adjacent to, but not directly at, somatomotor network (as shown previously by Kipping and colleagues [Kipping et al., 2013]).
evidence: Stated in the discussion and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 5.

claim: Connectivity from second motor representation engages areas adjacent to, but not directly at, somatomotor network.
source: These analyses are shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 5: while connectivity from first motor representation corresponds to cerebral cortical somatomotor network, connectivity from second motor representation engages areas adjacent to, but not directly at, somatomotor network (as shown previously by Kipping and colleagues [Kipping et al., 2013]).
evidence: Stated in the discussion, shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 5, and supported by citation to Kipping et al.

claim: Connectivity from first/second task-focused nonmotor representation corresponds to cerebral cortical task-positive networks.
source: Similarly, while connectivity from first/second task-focused nonmotor representation corresponds to cerebral cortical task-positive networks, connectivity from third task-focused nonmotor representation engages areas adjacent to, but not directly at, task-positive networks.
evidence: Stated in the discussion.

claim: Connectivity from third task-focused nonmotor representation engages areas adjacent to, but not directly at, task-positive networks.
source: Similarly, while connectivity from first/second task-focused nonmotor representation corresponds to cerebral cortical task-positive networks, connectivity from third task-focused nonmotor representation engages areas adjacent to, but not directly at, task-positive networks.
evidence: Stated in the discussion.

claim: Connectivity from first/second task-unfocused nonmotor representation corresponds to cerebral cortical task-negative networks (Default Mode Network).
source: Following the same logic, while connectivity from first/second task-unfocused nonmotor representation corresponds to cerebral cortical task-negative networks (Default Mode Network), connectivity from third task-focused nonmotor representation engages areas adjacent to, but not directly at, task-negative networks.
evidence: Stated in the discussion.

claim: Connectivity from third task-focused nonmotor representation engages areas adjacent to, but not directly at, task-negative networks.
source: Following the same logic, while connectivity from first/second task-unfocused nonmotor representation corresponds to cerebral cortical task-negative networks (Default Mode Network), connectivity from third task-focused nonmotor representation engages areas adjacent to, but not directly at, task-negative networks.
evidence: Stated in the discussion.

claim: Data-driven clustering of the first two gradients resulted in a division of gradients 1 and 2 in three areas encompassing the High-G1/High-G2/Low-G1 parcellation.
source: A data-driven clustering of the first two gradients resulted in a division of gradients 1 and 2 in three areas encompassing our High-G1/High-G2/Low-G1 parcellation (Figure 3—figure supplement 3), further supporting this hypothesis-driven division.
evidence: Directly stated and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: The same relationship between the two motor and three nonmotor areas of representation was observed in the analysis of a single subject with only one resting-state run of 15 min.
source: The same relationship between the two motor and three nonmotor areas of representation was observed in the analysis of a single subject with only one resting-state run of 15 min (Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Directly stated and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4.
